title: A Bucket of Blood

evidence.note: Published in 1959, so public domain status would depend on a missing copyright notice or a missing renewal in the 1986-1987 window. I did not check the Catalog of Copyright Entries renewal volumes or the Copyright Office public records this session, so there is no primary evidence either way. This Internet Archive item (a-bucket-of-blood-1959) shows the Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, http://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/. That is the uploader's claim, not evidence.

This second Internet Archive item (BucketOfBlood720p1959) shows the CC0 1.0 Universal licence URL, http://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/. That is also the uploader's claim, not evidence of copyright status.

Wikipedia credits Fred Katz as composer. A sound film's recorded track normally shares the film's status, so the score likely follows the print, but the print status is itself unconfirmed. I did not check for a separate music registration or renewal.

Wikipedia credits the screenplay to Charles B. Griffith. I did not confirm whether it was an original work or whether a separate screenplay registration exists. The same Wikipedia article says the film was remade for television in 1995 and describes stage musical adaptations (Chicago's Annoyance Theatre in 2009, and La Mirada Theatre in 2023). Those are separate derivative works.

I did not find a documented restoration. The a-bucket-of-blood-1959 Internet Archive item is described by its uploader as an HD 1080p scan. Any added material on a commercial release could carry its own protection.

editorial:
A Bucket of Blood is Roger Corman's 1959 black comedy about a dim-witted busboy who finds acclaim as an artist when a plaster-covered dead cat is mistaken for a skillful statuette, then keeps producing 'sculptures' by increasingly deadly means. Dick Miller, Barboura Morris and Antony Carbone star, Charles B. Griffith wrote the screenplay, Fred Katz composed the score, Alta Vista Productions made it and American International Pictures distributed it. The uploader's description on one Internet Archive scan says it was shot in a few days on leftover sets from Diary of a High-School Bride, and that the same sets were used a few days later for The Little Shop of Horrors.

The rights trap is that the copyright status is unconfirmed. The film was published in 1959, so a renewal was due in 1986 or 1987, and I did not verify either a renewal or its absence in primary records. The Internet Archive's Public Domain Mark (one item) and CC0 label (the other item) are uploader claims. Before commercial reuse, search the Copyright Office public records and the CCE renewal volumes for 1986 and 1987 yourself. The 1995 TV remake and the stage musicals described on Wikipedia are separate works with their own rights.
faq: Is A Bucket of Blood in the public domain?

Unconfirmed. One Internet Archive item is labelled Public Domain Mark and another is labelled CC0, but those are uploader labels. I did not verify a missing notice or a missing renewal in primary records. Check the Copyright Office public records and the CCE renewal volumes for 1986-1987 before relying on it.
Can I use the Internet Archive copy in a commercial project?

Not safely until the renewal check is done. The upload's public-domain label is the uploader's claim. The 1995 TV remake and the stage adaptations are separate works and are not covered by the original film's status.
